text:
How to choose colours
  A practical order of operations for picking colours — decide the job, choose on all three dials, then set the areas — and an honest account of why the named schemes explain much less than they claim.

  
    Termcolour harmony / colour scheme
    Also calledcolour harmony, colour schemes, palette design, choosing a palette, orange and teal
    Not the same asharmony vs contrast, hue schemes vs full colour design, the colour wheel as a mixing tool vs as a design tool
    Read10 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        First decide what the colour is forThen choose on all three dials, not on hueArea is the variable no scheme recordsLightness arrives whether you asked for it or notOne light does the unifying for freeThe named schemes, honestlyCheck the choice, do not trust itCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Photograph a desk with a red mug, a green plant, a blue notebook and a yellow sticky note. Four strong colours, evenly spread, and the picture is a mess. Now take almost any frame of Coco: two colours, one of them small and burning, and it reads as composed on purpose.
Most people explain the difference by naming a scheme — complementary, triadic, split-complementary. Learn the vocabulary, then learn that it decides almost nothing. Here is the order the decisions actually come in.
First decide what the colour is for
Handprint's definition is the most useful sentence in the literature: colour harmony is the manipulation of lightness and chroma within a given selection of hues so that all colours contribute to an intended visual effect. Everything hangs on the last three words, and the effects pull against each other:

Separation. Keeping a figure legible against its ground. Wants a large gap on some dial; lightness is the reliable one.
Cohesion. Making things read as belonging together — a costume, a brand, a room. Wants a narrow range, and hue is where you narrow it.
Mood. Making the picture feel like a place and a time. Wants a plausible light, which constrains all three dials at once.

A palette that separates beautifully will often fail to cohere, so name the job first.
Then choose on all three dials, not on hue
Handprint's conclusion after several hundred pages is that hue barely constrains you: given the right combination of chroma and lightness, any selection of hues can be made harmonious in terms of almost any intended contrast or design effect. Lightness and chroma are the powerful stimuli, and the most dependable move in the subject follows from that. A small patch of high chroma against a large low-chroma field takes the eye, every time — a hierarchy effect rather than a colour-theory one, since swapping the chroma gap for a lightness gap works identically. See Visual hierarchy.



Claude Monet, Impression, soleil levant, 1872. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. Public domain.
The extreme case of the lever. The sun disc covers about a thousandth of the canvas, plus a thin column of the same orange broken across the water. Everything else — masts, cranes, the whole sky below the top band — is low-chroma blue-green grey.
Measure it instead of guessing. The disc runs about L* 68 at chroma 67, the mist either side of it L* 50 at chroma 10. Follow the orange column down onto the water and the lightness advantage nearly disappears — those strokes sit at L* 52 against water at L* 45 — while the chroma gap holds at roughly 48 against 15. Chroma, not value, is what points this picture at one spot.


The reverse is where most amateur palettes die: large areas of high chroma fight.


Two hues, low chroma: Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Silver — Chelsea, 1871
Three hues, high chroma: Van Gogh, The Night Café, 1888


Two public-domain paintings seventeen years apart, differing mainly in how much chroma is allowed and over how much area. Right: Yale University Art Gallery.
Whistler works one hue. River, far bank, sky and the moored barge are all a blue, and the picture is separated by lightness alone. Count the exceptions: two orange lamp notes, each a few millimetres of paint with a short reflection under it. Those are the only marks in the frame with any chroma, and they carry the whole evening.
Van Gogh does the opposite deliberately, and wrote to Theo that he had tried to express "the terrible passions of humanity" with red and green. The wall is a large field of near-maximum red, the ceiling and billiard table near-maximum green, the floor yellow. No area yields, so the eye is pulled round the room and never settles. Not a mistake — it is what large opposed chroma does.


Area is the variable no scheme records
A scheme names hues and never says how much of each. That is the omission that matters most: the same two colours go from fighting to working on area alone.

50%50%the same two colours in both panelsL* 64, chroma 84, hues 140° and 320°Equal areaneither half can be the subject, and theedge between them has nothing to resolve90%10%the same two colours in both panelsL* 64, chroma 84, hues 140° and 320°One tenth the areathe green is now a field and the violetan accent — a hierarchy, not a new palette

Identical colours in both panels — same lightness, same chroma, hues 180° apart — so area is the only thing that changes.
Left, half and half. Neither can be the subject and neither can be the ground, so the edge between them has nothing to resolve and starts to buzz.
Right, one tenth. Instantly a field and an accent. Nothing was recoloured; a hierarchy was simply declared.


Munsell put a number on it in 1921. Call a colour's strength its value times its chroma, then give the weaker colour the larger area in inverse proportion: a muted dark blue at value 4, chroma 2 has strength 8, a muted orange-yellow at value 8, chroma 4 has strength 32, so the blue covers roughly four times the area. Which reduces to a maxim worth carrying — a large field can be luminous in lightness or in chroma, but not both.
Lightness arrives whether you asked for it or not
Pure hues sit at different lightnesses — yellow at full strength is light, violet dark — so a pair chosen on hue alone drags a value contrast in with it.

Six pairs on the wheelthe wheel has one axis, hue, so all sixread as the same relationship: 180° apartand therefore interchangeable0255075100lightness L*8orange /blue28red /cyan37cyan /rose40yellow /blue41green /violet55yellow green /violetΔL*The same six pairs, measuredeach hue at the strongest chroma sRGB canshow. The value gap you get for free runsfrom 8 points to 55, and you did not pick it

Left, six complementary pairs as a wheel shows them: six diameters, all 180°, apparently the same relationship six times over.
Right, the same twelve colours plotted against measured lightness, each at the strongest chroma sRGB can display. The free value gap runs from 8 points for orange against blue to 55 points for yellow-green against violet — nearly the whole scale. Notice the chroma columns too: red reaches chroma 105 while its opposite cyan tops out near 44, so the pair cannot even be matched in strength.


Hence the rule that you cannot put a saturated yellow in a dark passage — see Hue, value and chroma.
One light does the unifying for free
The strongest unifier available is not a scheme, it is a shared light source. Under one tinted light every surface shifts toward the light's hue, the opposite hue neutralises toward grey, and the total spread of colour shrinks — which is the description of a monochromatic palette. Weaken the tint and you get an analogous one; bright neutral light gives the wide spread people call triadic. Which is why photographs taken in one light look harmonious for free, and most of why the schemes feel right at all. See The colour of the light. Note the one scheme it leaves out: two strong lights of opposite colour on opposite sides of an object is stage lighting, not weather — hence orange-and-teal reading as cinematic rather than real.
The named schemes, honestly
Analogous, complementary, split-complementary, triadic. Keep them for one good reason: they stop a beginner centring everything on one hue, and force a decision about how wide the palette is.
What they cannot do is predict the result. They are stated as pure hue relationships, deliberately independent of which hues we are talking about — spin the dial and the recipe is unchanged.



Paul Gauguin, Bouquet de fleurs, 1897. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. Public domain. Handprint uses this painting to work through colour design, so it is the fairest test of the schemes.
Name the palette and you get scarlet, umber, ochre, blue-grey — which sounds like a scheme and tells you nothing. The information is in the area and the chroma. Measured off this reproduction, the scarlet marks cover about 3.5 per cent of the canvas and 94 per cent of the surface sits below chroma 45: the ochre wall is chroma 26, the blue-grey cloth 12, the dark leaves under 10.
Handprint then ran the experiment. He rotated every hue in this painting one step around the circle, once toward magenta and once toward green. The "scheme" is identical in all three versions and both rotations fall apart: one trades the scarlet-against-umber punch for a limp red-against-maroon, the other turns the light sickly. If the relationship were doing the work, spinning the dial would be free.


His diagnosis is the line to keep: the colour space is not as symmetrical as a circle or as homogeneous as cookie dough, so cookie-cutter concepts will not get you far. And "complementary" alone names four unrelated results — see Complementary colours.
Check the choice, do not trust it

Convert to greyscale. If the structure collapses without hue, no palette will rescue it — see Value structure. Then shrink it to a thumbnail: an accent that dies at 5 per cent of full width was never an accent.
Simulate red-green colour deficiency. Around one man in twelve of northern European descent has some form of it, so a distinction carried by red against green alone needs a lightness or shape difference underneath it.
Cover the neighbours of any colour you are about to call wrong. Not fussiness:


patch #9B9B9B · L* 64, chroma 0The same grey on bluefield #547BC7 · L* 52, chroma 45patch #9B9B9B · L* 64, chroma 0The same grey on orangefield #AE6D38 · L* 52, chroma 45

The two grey squares are the same colour. Both are #9B9B9B — L* 64, chroma 0, a pure neutral with no hue in it at all. The fields are matched too: identical L* 52 and identical chroma 45, differing only in hue angle, so no lightness contrast is doing the work.
The grey on blue reads faintly warm, the grey on orange faintly cool. Chevreul catalogued the effect in 1839 and it has not budged since. The consequence is severe: a colour has no appearance on its own. Two swatches compared in different surroundings are not comparable at all.


Common mistakes

"Harmony is about hue." Hue is the part the diagrams show. Lightness, chroma and relative area do most of the work and appear in none of them.
"It clashes, so a colour is wrong." Far more often the proportions are wrong, or the two sit at the same value with nothing to separate them.
"More hues means a richer picture." Ruskin's rule runs the other way: the less colour you do the work with, the better it will always be.
"Discord means I got it wrong." Ruskin again: "If ever any scientific person tells you that two colours are 'discordant', make a note of the two colours, and put them together whenever you can." Brejon's team made a night sky green rather than blue in Playmobil because green is uncomfortable, and discomfort was the point.


Picking a palette in five steps

Say the job out loud: separate, cohere, or set a mood.
Choose the value structure first, in greyscale, before any hue exists.
Pick the hue family, then decide where the one high-chroma passage goes, and how small.
Set the areas. Two strong colours near 50/50? Give one a tenth of the frame and see whether the hues were ever the problem.
Ask whether this palette could come from a real light. If not, that is a style choice — say so rather than calling it wrong.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Hue, value and chroma
              A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
            
          
        
          
            
              Complementary colours
              The pair of colours that cancel each other. There are two different pairs answering to that name — the one that mixes to grey and the one your eye pairs — and they are almost never the same colour.
            
          
        
          
            
              The colour wheel, and why there is more than one
              A ring of hues in spectral order, closed at the join by colours no wavelength can make. It is a working model, not a picture of light — and different jobs need different wheels, which is why they disagree about what sits opposite what.
            
          
        
          
            
              The colour of the light
              What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.
